la:noun:metus.html:
mĕtus, ūs, m. (
fem.: nulla in me est metus, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Müll.: metus ulla, id. ap. ; cf. Ann. v. 537, and Trag. v. 179 Vahl.; dat. metu, ; ), fear, dread, apprehension, anxiety; constr. with gen. object., with ne, with acc. and inf.
Lit.: est metus futurae aegritudinis sollicita exspectatio,; cf. : metum excitari vel propriis vel communibus periculis,: in metu esse,to be in fear, be fearful,: est et in metu peregrinantium, ut, etc.,they are also afraid,: mihi etiam unum de malis in metu est, fratris miseri negotium,a subject of fear,: metum habere,to entertain fear, be afraid,: metum concipere,to become afraid,: capere,: accipere,: metum facere alicui, to make afraid, put in fear, frighten,

5, 10, 28: metum inicere,: incutere, Cael. ap. : inferre,: affere,: offerre,: obicere,: intentare,: metu territare,to alarm greatly, fill with fear,: metum pati,: alicui adimere,to take away, remove,: metu exonerare,to relieve from fear,: removere metum,to take away, remove,: levare alicui,: alicui deicere,: solvere,to remove, dismiss,: civitati metum, formidinem oblivionem inicere, Ser. Samm. ap. : metu et impressione alicujus terroris mentiri,: metu mortis furem occidere, Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 7, 3, 3: quis metus aut pudor est umquam properantis avari?: reddere metu, non moribus,.— Poet. in plur., .—

With gen. object.: vulnerum metus,: ne reliquos populares metus invaderet parendi sibi,: id bellum excitabat metus Pompei victoris Hiempsalem in regnum restituentis,; v. ; : propter metum alicujus, for fear of: Judaeorum,; .—
With ne: quod ubi Romam est nuntiatum, senatui metum injecit, ne, etc.,: ne lassescat fortuna, metus est,.—
With acc. and inf.: quantus metus est mihi, venire huc salvum nunc patruum!.—(ε) With ab: metus a praetore Romano,; ; ; cf.: metus poenae a Romanis,; .—(ζ) With pro: metus pro universā republicā,.—(η) With ex: metus ex imperatore,.—
Poet., religious awe, holy dread: laurus Sacra comam multosque metu servata per annos,.—Poetic awe: evoe! recenti mens trepidat metu,.—
Transf.
Conor., a cause of fear, a terror (poet.): metus Libyci,i. e. the head of Medusa,: nulli nocte metus,alarms,.—
Personified: Mĕtus, the god of fear or terror, ; ; .

senses: to be anxious or afraid about or for a specific person or thing
la:verb:metuo.html:
mĕtŭo, ŭi, ūtum (cf.:
nimis ante metutum,), 3, v. a. and n.
metus
, to fear, be afraid of a person or thing; to hesitate, not to venture, not to wish (syn.: vereor, formido, timeo); with inf., with ne, to fear lest; with ui or ne non, to fear that not; also of inanimate things, with acc., to fear, revere, reverence one; as a v. n., to fear, be afraid, be in fear, be apprehensive, esp. as the effect of the idea of threatening evil (whereas timere usually denotes the effect of some external cause of terror); to dread, apprehend; with an indirect interrogation: non metuo quin, for non dubito quin, I doubt not but; to be anxious about any one; with dat. (class.).
Act.: quem metuont oderunt, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 403 Vahl.): deos et amo et metuo,: male ego metuo milvos,: metuebant (senem) servi, verebantur liberi,: tu, qui crimen ais te metuisse,: nec pol istae metuunt Deos, : absentem patrem,: nec metuit quemquam,.—With ab: quid a nobis metuit?: a me insidias,: supplicia a vobis metuere debent,to fear from you,: a quo (Ajace) sibi non injuriā summum periculum metuebat,: a quo domino sibi metuebat graves cruciatus,; Gregor. M. Homil. 1, 14, 2; Aug. cont. Acad. 2, 8.—With ex: si periculum ex illis metuit,.—With de: de lanificio neminem metuo, una aetate quae sit,i. e. no one's competition in spinning,.—Of inanim. subjects: quae res cotidie videntur, minus metuunt furem,.—
With inf.: metuont credere omnes,: ut tentare spem certaminis metuunt,: nil metuunt jurare,: reddere soldum,not to wish, be averse to,: praebere,.—Of nonpersonal subjects: illum aget pennā metuente solvi Fama superstes,. —
With ne: nimis metuebam male, ne abiisses,: male metuo ne ... morbus aggravescat,: fratrem, ne intus sit (Gr. construction),.—
With ut: ornamenta, quae locavi, metuo, ut possim recipere,: metuo ut hodie possim emolirier,: metuo ut substet hospes,: ut sis vitalis,.—(ε) With ne non: metuo ne non sit surda,; : metuis ne non, quom velis, convincas esse illum tuom?.—(ξ) With quin: non metuo meae quin uxori latae suppetiae sient,.—(η) With object-clause, to await with fear, anxiety; to be in apprehension, concerned about: metuo, patres quot fuerint,: metui, quid futurum denique esset,I dreaded, awaited with fear,: metuo quid agam. Sy. Metuis? quasi non ea potestas sit tua, etc., : metuo qualem tu me esse hominem existumes,.—(θ) Pass. with dat.: jam maturis metuendus Juppiter uvis,. —(ι) Absol.: se e contempto metuendum fecit,.—
(Eccl. Lat.) Of religious fear, to revere, dread, hold in reverence: Deum,: Dominum Deum nostrum,: sanctuarium meum,.—
Neutr., to fear, be afraid, be apprehensive, etc.
With de: neque tam de suā vitā, quam de me metuit,fears not so much for his own life as for me,.—
With ab: metuens ab Hannibale,afraid of Hannibal,.—
With pro: metuere pro aliquo,.—
With dat., to be anxious about or for a person or thing: metuens pueris,: inopi metuens formica senectae,: tum decuit metuisse tuis,.—Hence, mĕtŭens, entis, P. a., fearing, afraid of any thing; anxious for any person or thing; with gen. or absol. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): contentus parvo metuensque futuri,: metuens virgae,.—Comp.: quo non metuentius ullum Numinis ingenium,: Nero metuentior in posterum,.
la:verb:metuo.inflection: ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a. and n.

la:verb:metior.html:
mētĭor, mensus (post-class. metītus, ), 4, v. dep.
Sanscr. ma, to measure; cf. Gr. μέ-τρον, Lat. modus
,
to measure, mete (lands, corn); also, to measure or mete out, to deal out, distribute by measure (class.).
Lit.: metiri agrum,: frumentum,: sol, quem metiri non possunt,: magnitudinem mundi,: nummos, to measure one's money, i. e. to have a great abundance of it, : nummos modio,: se ad candelabrum,: pedes syllabis,to measure by syllables,: frumentum militibus metiri,: cum exercitu frumentum metiri oporteret,; 7, 71: Caecubum,: quis mensus est pugillo aquas?: tantus acervus fuit, ut metientibus dimidium super tres modios explesse, sint quidam auctores,.—
Poet. transf., to measure a distance, i. e. to pass, walk, or sail through or over, to traverse: Sacram metiente te viam (of the measured pace of a proud person),: aequor curru,to sail through,: aquas carinā,: tu, cursu, dea menstruo metiens iter annuom,to go through complete,: instabili gressu metitur litora cornix,.—Also absol.: quin hic metimur gradibus militariis,to walk,.—
Trop., to measure, estimate, judge one thing by another; also simply to measure, estimate, judge of, set a value on a thing.
With abl. of the standard of comparison, or the means of judgment: sonantia metiri auribus,: oculo latus,: omnia quaestu,by profit,: qui nihil alterius causa faciet et metietur suis commodis omnia,: vides igitur, si amicitiam sua caritate metiare, nihil esse praestantius,: vim eloquentiae sua facultate non rei natura,: omnia voluptate,: studia utilitate,: magnos homines virtute, non fortuna,: usum pecuniae non magnitudine, sed ratione,: officia utilitate,: odium in se aliorum suo in eos metiens odio,: pericula suo metu,: peccata vitiis,: aetatem nostram non spatio senectutis, sed tempore adulescentiae,.—
With ex (very rare): fidelitas, quam ego ex mea conscientiā metior,: ex eo, quantum cuique satis est, metiuntur homines divitiarum modum, .—
With ad: nec se metitur ad illum quem dedit haec (paupertas) posuitque modum,i. e. accommodates herself,.—
Absol. (post-Aug.): metiri ac diligenter aestimare vires suas,: pondera sua,: sua regna,. —(ε) With quod: quanto metiris pretio, quod, etc.,.—
To traverse. go over, pass through: late Aequora prospectu metior alta meo,: tot casus, tot avia,: jamque duas lucis partes Hyperione menso,.—
To measure out, deal to any one, treat one well or ill: mensurā quā mensi fueritis, remetietur vobis,; cf. .!*? In pass. signif., to be measured: agri glebatim metiebantur,: an sol pedis unius latitudine metiatur,.—Part. perf.: mensus, a, um, measured off: mensa spatia conficere,.—As subst.: bene mensum dabo,good measure,.

senses: turning point, winning post (pillar at each end of the Circus route)
la:noun:meta.html:
mēta, ae, f.
root ma-, measure, whence Gr. μέτρον; Lat. manus, mane, etc. (q. v.), properly, that which marks a measured space, hence
,
any mark at a boundary or limit, esp.,
The conical columns set in the ground at each end of the Roman Circus, the goal, turning-post: metaque fervidis Evitata rotis,: aut prius infecto deposcit praemia cursu Septima quam metam triverit ante rota,; cf.: et modo lora dabo, modo verbere terga notabo, Nunc stringam metas interiore rotā,; : petra in metae maxime modum erecta est, cujus ima spatiosiora sunt, altiora in artius coëunt, summa in acutum cacumen exsurgunt,i. e. in the shape of a cone,; cf. III. 3. infra).—
Any goal or winning-post, the mark, goal, in any contest of speed: optatam cursu contingere metam, of a footrace,: metam tenere, in a boatrace,.—
Trop. (because of the danger to drivers of striking the goal, and breaking their oars), a critical point, place of danger: fama adulescentis paulum haesit ad metas, notitiā novā mulieris,broke down, failed, at the critical point,.—
Transf., an end, period, extremity, boundary, limit: longarum haec meta viarum,: ad metas aevi pervenire,: metam tangere vitae,: ad metam properare,: ultima,: hic tibi mortis erant metae,: ad quas metas naturae sit perveniendum usu,i. e. extremes,: quando illa (luna) incurrat in umbram terrae, quae est meta noctis, eam obscurari necesse est,the limit, measure of night, (but v. 3. below, fin. and the passage there cited from Pliny): sol ex aequo metā distabat utrāque, equally far from both ends of his course, i. e. at noon, : intercalariis mensibus interponendis ita dispensavit (Numa), ut vices uno anno ad metam eandem solis unde orsi essent ... dies congruerent, Weissenb. ad loc.: metae Marsicae, = fines Marsorum, Kapp: pares horarum metas, tam antemeridialium quam postremarum, manifestant,.—
A turning-point in one's course: praestat Trinacrii metas lustrare Pachyni,to sail around the promontory of Pachynus,.—
Of any thing resembling in shape the meta of the Circus; any thing of a conical or pyramidal form, a cone, pyramid (class.); of a conical hill: ipse collis est in modum metae, in acutum cacumen a fundo satis lato fastigatus,: buxus in metas emittitur,into cones,: in metas foenum exstruere,in ricks, haycocks,: lactantes,conical cheeses,: lactis,: meta sudans,a conical stone on a fountain, dripping with water,: meta molendaria, or molendinaria, that part of the upper millstone which projects downward and grinds the corn (the upper part is the catillus, q. v.); = Gr. ὄνος ἀλέτης, : metas molendinarias rotare,: si minor materia quam lux, metae existere effigiem,i. e. if the solid body be smaller than the light, its shadow will be conical, (cf. the context).

la:noun:metallum.gloss: metal (atomic element or material made of such atoms)
senses: metal (atomic element or material made of such atoms)
precious metals, especially gold or silver.
la:noun:metallum.html:
mĕtallum, i, n., = μέταλλον,
a mine or quarry, of gold, silver, iron, or stone; voc. metalle, as if from metallus, .
Lit., the place where metals are dug, a mine: metalla vetera intermissa recoluit, et nova multis locis instituit,: sandaracae,: aurifera,gold-mines,: silicum,stone-quarry,: miniarium,: praeter annuum, quod ex metallis regiis capia, vectigal,: herba tantae suavitatis, ut metallum esse coeperit, a mine, i. e. that a tax was raised from it as from a mine, : damnare in metallum, to condemn to labor in the mines or quarries: damnatus in metallum,: condemnare aliquem ad metalla,: mediocrium delictorum poenae sunt metallum, ludus, deportatio,; : dare aliquem in metallum,: metallo plecti,: puniri,.—
Transf., the product of a mine or quarry.
A metal, as gold, silver, or iron: ubicumque una inventa vena argenti est, non procul invenitur alia. Hoc quidem et in omni fere materia: unde metalla Graeci videntur dixisse,. 6, 31, § 96: auri,: potior metallis libertas,i. e. gold and silver,: aeris,: pejoraque saecula ferri temporibus, quorum ... nomen a nullo posuit natura metallo,.—
Other things dug from the earth.
Marble, .—
Precious stone: radiantium metalla gemmarum,.—
Chalk: admiscetur creta ... Campani negant alicam confici sine eo metallo posse,.—
Sulphur: utque est ingenium vivacis metalli (sulphuris),. p. 228, 23.—(ε) Salt: metallum fragile,.—
Trop., metal, stuff, material: saecula meliore metallo,: mores meliore metallo,.

mētor, ātus, 1, v. dep.
